turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am afraid that a residence in Belgrave Square, though an undeniably desirable address, does not in itself guarantee the social standing necessary for a match of your daughter's stature. Tell me, Mr. Worthing, what is your profession?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am a gentleman farmer, Lady Bracknell. My profession is to provide for my household and to be a model citizen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A gentleman farmer, indeed? Mr. Worthing, farming is a respectable occupation, but it does not align with the social aspirations of my daughter. Tell me, do you have any significant connections or influence in the social circles that matter?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I must admit, Lady Bracknell, that my connections are limited to my immediate circle and the community in which I live. However, I am eager to learn and to grow in all areas that would be beneficial to your daughter and to me.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I see, Mr. Worthing. However, it seems your current status and connections fall short of what my daughter deserves. I must ask, do you have any plans to acquire the means and influence necessary to meet the expectations of our society?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, I cannot help but feel that your inquiries are rather narrow-minded. Mr. Worthing is a gentleman and a man of character. His status should not be the only measure of his worth.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am grateful for your support, Gwendolen. And to Lady Bracknell, I assure you that I am committed to doing everything in my power to meet the expectations you have set. My intentions are honourable, and I will strive to be a worthy husband for your daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, you are being rather unreasonable. Mr. Worthing's character and intentions are more important than his current status. I will not let these superficial matters come between us.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: My dear Gwendolen, your enthusiasm is commendable, but your understanding of the world is somewhat limited. Mr. Worthing, I must insist that you provide me with a more substantial plan to elevate your standing in society. Your current circumstances are not satisfactory.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, your insistence on superficial matters is disappointing. Mr. Worthing is a man of integrity and I refuse to let your standards dictate my happiness.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I understand your concerns and I will do my utmost to address them. I promise to work diligently to improve my standing and to ensure that I am a worthy partner for Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your promises are not sufficient. I require concrete evidence of your ability to provide Gwendolen with the lifestyle and social standing befitting a lady of her breeding.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I understand your requirements and I assure you, I am committed to meeting them. I will work hard to improve my circumstances and provide Gwendolen with everything she deserves.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I appreciate your assurances, Mr. Worthing, but mere words will not suffice. I require tangible proof of your capability to support my daughter in the manner to which she is accustomed.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I understand your need for evidence. I will do everything in my power to provide it. Please give me a chance to prove myself worthy of Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, I am well aware of your assurances. However, I must insist on immediate and substantial evidence of your financial stability and social connections. Merely promising to improve your circumstances is insufficient.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I understand your concerns and I will do my best to provide the evidence you seek. Please allow me the opportunity to demonstrate my commitment to Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, while your words are commendable, they lack the concrete evidence I require. I shall be expecting a detailed presentation of your financial standing and social connections at our next meeting.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I will prepare all the necessary documents and evidence for our next meeting. I am committed to Gwendolen and will do whatever it takes to satisfy your requirements.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Very well, Mr. Worthing. Until you can provide me with the necessary proof, I must reserve my judgment regarding your suitability as a husband for my daughter. Do not keep me waiting for long.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I dons depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
